title: Scientists See Tiny Particles Make Ripples in the Universe's First 'Soup'
summary:
Right after the universe began, it was trillions of degrees hot. Tiny particles called quarks and gluons zipped around at nearly the speed of light in a state of matter called quark-gluon plasma. It lasted only a few millionths of a second. Then it cooled, and the particles joined to form protons, neutrons and other building blocks of everything around us.

Today, physicists can make tiny amounts of this plasma at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland. They smash heavy atoms, such as lead, together at nearly the speed of light. The plasma droplets last less than a quadrillionth of a second.

Now a team led by physicists from MIT has found clear evidence that quarks leave wakes as they move through the plasma, like a duck making ripples on a pond. That means the plasma acts like one connected liquid, with waves, splashes and swirls, instead of a crowd of separate bouncing particles.

"It has been a long debate in our field, on whether the plasma should respond to a quark," said MIT physics professor Yen-Jie Lee. "Now we see the plasma is incredibly dense, such that it is able to slow down a quark, and produces splashes and swirls like a liquid."

Scientists think quark-gluon plasma was the universe's first liquid, and the hottest liquid ever known. It flows so smoothly, with almost no friction, that some call it a near-"perfect" liquid.

Earlier searches were tricky because quarks often appear in pairs moving in opposite directions, and one can hide the other's wake. The team developed a new method to spot the wakes.

By measuring how big the wakes get and how fast they fade, scientists hope to learn more about the universe's first moments. The findings appear in the journal Physics Letters B.
why_it_matters: Studying this plasma helps scientists understand how the matter that makes up everything around us first formed. It also tests long-debated ideas about how this early matter behaves.

background_read: All ordinary matter is made of atoms, and the protons and neutrons inside atoms are made of even smaller particles called quarks, held together by gluons.
Right after the Big Bang, the universe was so hot that quarks and gluons could not stick together and instead formed a hot plasma.
CERN's Large Hadron Collider is a huge ring-shaped machine that speeds up particles and smashes them together so scientists can study what comes out.
By recreating this plasma for tiny fractions of a second, physicists can learn how the early universe behaved.
